The Figure, Torah Teaching and Public Work of Rabbi Meir the Great of Premishlan
This text surveys the life and contribution of Rabbi Meir the Great of Premishlan, of the founding generation of the Hasidic movement and a disciple of the Besht. The article sketches his figure as one who fused deep kabbalistic scholarship with extreme humility, while detailing his illustrious family lineage, his work as an honest merchant and his later withdrawal to a life of the spirit. On the public plane, the text emphasizes his struggle against the Frankist sect and his role in the institutionalization of Hasidism in Galicia, alongside a presentation of his concealed books and the historical discussion surrounding his attempt to emigrate to the Land of Israel. Finally, the work analyzes the development of the Hasidic dynasty through a comparison between the hidden and mystical figure of the grandfather and the folk, popular leadership of his grandson, Rabbi Meirel.
The Figure, Torah Teaching and Public Work of Rabbi Meir the Great of Premishlan
Introduction: The Place of Rabbi Meir the Great at the Beginning of the Hasidic Movement
Rabbi Meir (the Great) of Premishlan (5463, 1703 – 22 Av 5533, 11 August 1773) is counted among the most formative and central figures of the founding generation of the Hasidic movement [cite: 1]. As a close companion and principal disciple of the father of the movement, Rabbi Yisrael Baal Shem Tov (the Besht), Rabbi Meir was active in a critical period in which Hasidism was shaped not as an institutional framework but as a spiritual, ecstatic and intimate fellowship [cite: 1]. His figure combines in a fascinating way traditional scholarship, deep kabbalistic thought, active public work against tendencies of heresy, and extreme humility that was expressed in his willingness to act at the margins of the social hierarchy for the sake of spreading the Hasidic idea. Understanding the work and teaching of Rabbi Meir the Great is essential for deciphering the transition of Hasidism from a closed mystical fellowship to a spiritual enterprise with mass influence on Eastern European Jewry.
Biography, Family Lineage and Stations of Life
Rabbi Meir was born in 5463 (1703) in the town of Premishlan in Galicia [cite: 1]. He grew out of a family foundation with an exceptional Torah and mystical lineage. His father was Rabbi Yaakov "Tam" of Premishlan-Kolomyia, son of Rabbi David of Premishlan, who traced his descent directly to Rabbi Moshe "the Saraf" and to Rabbi Chaim Tzvi [cite: 1]. This line of descent is bound inseparably to Rabbi Yaakov HaLevi of Marvège-Corbeil, one of the great Tosafists in France and the author of the well-known book "She'elot u-Teshuvot min ha-Shamayim" (Responsa from Heaven) [cite: 1]. This historical link to one who wrote halakhic questions and answers on the basis of heavenly revelations and mystical dreams lends a deep context to Rabbi Meir's later engagement in the esoteric teaching and to his being regarded as possessing the holy spirit. Rabbi Meir's mother was the Rebbetzin Bat-Sheva [cite: 1].
In the first half of his life Rabbi Meir engaged in commerce, and excelled in exceptional integrity. His reliability in his business was so extraordinary that even the gentile population of the region called him admiringly "Meir the Faithful" [cite: 1]. This biographical aspect is not accidental; it reflects the early Hasidic conception of the holiness of work and of the ability to serve the Creator within the material world ("worship through corporeality").
The turning point in his life came when he was about 35 [cite: 1]. Rabbi Meir made a dramatic decision to withdraw completely from all his commercial affairs, to shut himself within the walls of the beit midrash and to devote all his time to Torah, to Kabbalah and to spiritual mortifications [cite: 1]. This withdrawal marked his transformation into a spiritual beacon, as multitudes of Hasidim and seekers of God began to stream to his door to hear his teaching and receive his blessings [cite: 1].
Rabbi Meir passed away on 22 Av 5533 (11 August 1773), at the age of about 70 [cite: 1]. Although there are sporadic opinions that place his death later, in 5541 (1781), the inscription on his tombstone in the Premishlan cemetery confirms the year 5533 as the historical date of death [cite: 1]. His grave became a site of pilgrimage, and in the 2000s his original tombstone was located and re-erected at the entrance of the cemetery by the "Ohalei Tzaddikim" committee headed by Yisrael Meir Gabbai [cite: 1]. After his death, his place was filled by his son, Rabbi Aharon Aryeh Leib of Premishlan [cite: 1].
The Connection with the Baal Shem Tov and the Struggle against the Frankist Sect
The relationship between Rabbi Meir the Great and Rabbi Yisrael Baal Shem Tov was founded on a deep ideological partnership and mutual esteem, Rabbi Meir being regarded as one of his very first disciples and closest companions [cite: 1]. This partnership was not merely theoretical, but found practical expression in the great public struggles of the period.
According to Hasidic tradition, Rabbi Meir stood at the side of the Besht in one of the hardest and most fateful struggles of the Jewry of Poland and Galicia at that time – the campaign to subdue the remnants of the Frankist sect in the city of Lvov [cite: 1]. This sect, under the leadership of Jacob Frank, constituted a direct continuation of late Sabbateanism, preaching antinomianism (the abolition of the commandments) and creating a deep religious and social rupture within the Jewish communities. Rabbi Meir's involvement in this struggle emphasizes that alongside his mystical inclination, he saw supreme importance in defending the boundaries of halakha and tradition and in preserving the integrity of the Jewish people against destructive influences.
After the passing of the Baal Shem Tov in 5560 (1760), a change took place in the leadership structure of the young Hasidic movement. Instead of following a single center of leadership, Rabbi Meir began to lead an independent community of his own in the town of Premishlan [cite: 1]. He thereby became one of the first Rebbes to institutionalize an independent Hasidic court in Galicia, and laid the foundations for the spread of Hasidism in this region [cite: 2].
The Controversy over Emigration to the Land of Israel: Cross-Checking and Historical Complexity
One of the fascinating traditions, which arouses wide scholarly and historiographical discussion, holds that Rabbi Meir the Great emigrated to the Land of Israel in 5524 (1764) [cite: 3]. This tradition poses a certain challenge to researchers, since it apparently clashes with the accepted tradition according to which he died and was buried in his town of Premishlan in 5533 (1773), where his tombstone was also found and re-erected at the entrance of the cemetery [cite: 1].
To reconcile this contradiction, scholars of Hasidism propose several directions of interpretation that combine the various historical aspects:
The Circle of Disciples and the Unique Model of Teaching
One of the most fascinating aspects of the work of Rabbi Meir the Great is his relationship with his disciples, and in particular with the famous kabbalist Rabbi Shabbetai of Rashkov [cite: 1, 4]. Rabbi Shabbetai, who was a scribe of Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot (sofer STaM) and a renowned kabbalist, became famous chiefly for editing the "Siddur of Rabbi Shabbetai of Rashkov" – a prayer book based on the kavvanot (mystical intentions) of the Arizal and the Besht [cite: 4, 5]. Rabbi Shabbetai accepted the authority of the Baal Shem Tov, but he called Rabbi Meir of Premishlan by the distinct title "mori" (my teacher) [cite: 4].
Despite Rabbi Meir's lofty spiritual standing as the teacher of the kabbalist of Rashkov, Hasidic history records a period in which Rabbi Meir stayed in the home of Rabbi Shabbetai and served there, of all things, in the simple role of a "melamed" (teacher) of young schoolchildren (tinokot shel beit rabban) [cite: 1]. This situation represents several deep tendencies in early Hasidism:
Breaking the institutional hierarchy: The choice of a spiritual leader of such magnitude to earn his living as a simple melamed in the home of his disciple attests to a rejection of the conception of communal authority and to the adoption of the value of humility in practice.
Connecting the hidden and the revealed: The melamed who deals with the letters of the alphabet with small children is also the kabbalist who delves into the most cosmic secrets. This corresponds directly to the teaching of the Besht concerning the holiness of the letters and of speech as a vehicle of divine revelation [cite: 5].
Unmediated connection: The creation of a spiritual fellowship in which the boundaries between teacher and disciple are blurred in favor of partnership in mystical worship and in copying kabbalistic writings [cite: 4].
His Torah Teaching and His Kabbalistic and Aggadic Works
The Torah teaching of Rabbi Meir the Great rests on two central pillars: the esoteric teaching (Kabbalah) and practical Hasidic thought [cite: 1]. Unlike many of his contemporaries who left their teaching only in oral form, Rabbi Meir was a prolific writer, but his writings met with a complex system of concealment and the hiding of secrets.
The Manuscripts and the Works Attributed to Him
Rabbi Meir composed a number of works that influenced the development of mystical thought in Hasidism:
"Ya'ir Or" (or "Meir Ya'ir"): This is Rabbi Meir's central and deepest work on Kabbalah [cite: 1]. The work deals with complex secrets of the esoteric teaching and remains in manuscript to this day [cite: 1]. According to a strict Hasidic tradition, there is a grave prohibition against printing this book and disseminating it publicly [cite: 1]. This prohibition reflects the historical fear of the leaders of Hasidism of an excessive popularization of Kabbalah, a fear that intensified in the wake of the crisis of Sabbateanism and Frankism, against which Rabbi Meir himself fought [cite: 1].
"Or Torato shel Rabbi Meir": Another book attributed to him, containing his homilies and explanations on the Torah [cite: 1]. Like "Ya'ir Or," this book too was not brought to print and has been preserved in manuscripts held by a select few [cite: 1].
"Or ha-Me'ir" and "Margenita de-Rabbi Meir": These books are collections in which his sayings, his oral teachings, and some of the hundreds of wonder tales and legends that spread about him and his descendants over the generations were gathered [cite: 1]. These books bridge the strict scholarly-kabbalistic world and popular Hasidic memory.
"Aspaklaria ha-Me'ira": A modern work in two volumes written by the author Mordechai Gerlitz (5757, 1996), the first two chapters of which are devoted to presenting a portrait of Rabbi Meir the Great and his deeds [cite: 1].
The Family and the Hasidic Dynasty
The work of Rabbi Meir the Great was not confined to his lifetime alone, but was perpetuated and expanded through his descendants, who established splendid Hasidic courts and spread his teaching throughout Eastern Europe [cite: 1, 2]. His sons and descendants combined mystical devotion with active communal leadership.

An Intergenerational Comparison: Rabbi Meir the Great versus His Grandson Rabbi Meir the Second
In order to understand the magnitude of the change that Hasidism as a whole underwent through the prism of the Premishlan dynasty, one must examine the differences and the connections between the founder, Rabbi Meir the Great, and his famous grandson, Rabbi Meir of Premishlan the Second (known by his epithet "Rabbi Meirel") [cite: 3, 6].

Historical and Conceptual Insights on the Transition of the Generations in Premishlan
An in-depth analysis of the development of the Premishlan dynasty reveals the broad historical process that the Hasidic movement as a whole underwent – from the status of a mystical, kabbalistic and closed sect to the status of a broad and accessible popular movement.
Rabbi Meir the Great represents the "hidden stage" of Hasidism. His written kabbalistic thought, as expressed in the book "Ya'ir Or," remained concealed in manuscript and forbidden to publication [cite: 1]. This restriction is not merely technical, but ideological: in the generation of Rabbi Meir the Great the esoteric teaching was still the possession of a select minority, and engagement in it required the utmost caution so as not to slide into Sabbatean messianic fantasies [cite: 1]. Rabbi Meir's conduct as a simple melamed in the home of his disciple attests to an attempt to preserve the traditional social harmony without being conspicuous or creating new centers of political power [cite: 1].
By contrast, his grandson Rabbi Meir the Second (Rabbi Meirel) was active in an era in which Hasidism had already become the dominant force on the Jewish street in Eastern Europe [cite: 3, 6]. At this stage, the spiritual energy that had been stored up in the grandfather's kabbalistic manuscripts was translated into social and emotional action: extreme distribution of charity, the performance of open wonders, and uncompromising protection of every Jew, even of those considered to be on the margins of society [cite: 6]. The wonders of the grandson were nothing but an externalization and popularization of the kabbalistic unifications (yichudim) of the grandfather. Through love of Israel and the simplification of mystical ideas into popular language, the grandson succeeded in making his grandfather's mystical legacy accessible to the masses, and thereby ensured the survival and long-term influence of the dynasty [cite: 3, 6].
Rabbi Meir the Great is thus the quiet architect of many splendid dynasties that issued from the loins of the Nadvorna, Kretshnif, Kalush and Glina Hasidic groups [cite: 1, 2]. His spiritual sowing of seeds, within the walls of the beit midrash in Premishlan and in the struggles alongside the Besht, is what made possible the growth of a splendid movement that changed the face of Jewish history [cite: 1, 2].
